description.appearance: Oval, green to yellowish body with two dark spots on the back; eight legs
description.life_cycle: Egg → larva → protonymph → deutonymph → adult; several generations per season
description.notes: Very small, often requires a hand lens or magnification for detection

secondary: Many ornamentals, vegetables, and fruit crops
weeds: Common weed hosts can harbor populations during off-season

distribution: Worldwide, especially in warm, dry conditions

foliage: Tiny yellow or pale spots on upper leaf surface (stippling)
Webbing on undersides of leaves under heavy infestations
Leaves may turn bronze, curl, and drop prematurely
symptoms.overall_impact: Reduced photosynthesis, stunted growth, lower yield, increased plant stress

conditions_for_development: Population growth is rapid under temperatures of 25–35°C
spread: Transported via infested plants or plant debris

cultural: Maintain adequate irrigation and humidity to reduce stress on plants
Remove infested plant debris and weeds
Avoid excessive use of broad-spectrum insecticides that disrupt natural predators
biological: Introduce predatory mites (e.g., Phytoseiulus persimilis, Neoseiulus californicus)
Encourage natural predators such as lady beetles and lacewings
chemical: Use miticides (acaricides) as a last resort and rotate chemical classes to avoid resistance
Apply to undersides of leaves where mites are concentrated

notes: One of the most common and economically important mite pests worldwide
Can develop resistance rapidly to multiple chemical classes
references: Helle, W. & Sabelis, M.W. (1985). Spider Mites: Their Biology, Natural Enemies and Control. Elsevier.
Gerson, U., Smiley, R.L., & Ochoa, R. (2003). Mites (Acari) for Pest Control. Blackwell Science.
Jeppson, L.R., Keifer, H.H., & Baker, E.W. (1975). Mites Injurious to Economic Plants. University of California Press.
